title: Choose input classes from the contract
goals: Partition a method’s inputs by the behaviour promised for them.
Pair every selected input with a precise expected result.
Explain why a test is black-box and what it can reveal.
setup: You can already write an assertion. The next decision is which call deserves an assertion. Black-box testing chooses cases from a public contract: parameters, documented behaviour and observable results. You do not need to read the implementation. An equivalence class groups inputs expected to follow the same rule. Testing a representative is useful evidence, not a guarantee about every member.
bridge: Classes tell you where behaviour differs. Next, test the exact places where one class meets another.
summary: Choose one input group at a time from a method’s promised behaviour.

flow.title: Choose from the promise
flow.html:
You can design a test without seeing a method body. This is black-box testing: the public contract supplies the input rules and expected results. Our familiar Numbers group now has a fee operation. Read its promise before deciding what value to pass.

/** Negative items: -1. Zero items: 0. Positive items: 5. */
static int fee(int items)

flow.title: Group inputs by their rule
flow.html:
An equivalence class is a group of inputs governed by the same expected-behaviour rule. This fee contract gives three groups. The grouping comes from behaviour, even though every argument has the same Java type, int. First name the groups; then choose concrete values.

GroupRule
NegativeReturn -1
ZeroReturn 0
PositiveReturn 5

flow.title: Choose a representative
flow.html:
A representative is one concrete input chosen from a group. Here -4 represents the negative class. Testing that value is evidence about that execution, not proof about all negative integers. Choose a value you can name and explain instead of writing only “test a negative number.”

assertEquals(-1, Numbers.fee(-4));

flow.title: Give the expectation an independent basis
flow.html:
The oracle is your basis for deciding whether the result is right. For this small method, the contract is the oracle. Write the expected constant from that rule. Calling the same method twice and comparing the answers could accept the same incorrect answer twice.

assertEquals(5, Numbers.fee(8));

flow.title: Notice a repeated group
flow.html:
Three different inputs do not necessarily test three different rules. Inputs 2, 8 and 20 are all positive here. They may have other useful purposes, but this set leaves the negative and zero rules untouched. Ask what each added case contributes to the suite.

InputExpected
25
85
205

flow.title: Separate the type from the value
flow.html:
An invalid business value can still be a valid Java argument. A negative count fits int, so fee can receive it and return its rejection result. The text "-4" has type String and cannot reach this int parameter as written. Apply the type check before the contract check.

Numbers.fee(-4)

flow.title: Name partial internal knowledge
flow.html:
Grey-box testing uses some internal knowledge along with the contract. Suppose you know a collection caches its count, although its full body is hidden. That knowledge can motivate checking the count after removal. The classification describes why you chose the case, not which assertion you used.

Information usedDesign basis
Public contract onlyBlack-box
Contract plus partial internal knowledgeGrey-box

flow.html:
Combine the decisions you have just practised: choose a group, choose a concrete input, and give its contract-based result. Each row should say why it exists. This is enough to plan a small black-box suite before writing test methods. Later you will strengthen it at the boundaries.

title: Test boundaries and shapes
goals: Derive boundary cases from inclusive and exclusive limits.
Choose non-square shapes that reveal row/column confusion.
Keep every other parameter valid while targeting one boundary.
setup: An implementation can handle an ordinary value correctly but get a boundary wrong. Boundary-value testing concentrates on the edges of an input class. For integer limits, “just below” and “just above” usually mean subtracting or adding one. For an array index, the last valid position is one less than its length.
bridge: Now apply the same discipline to references: a missing object, an empty object and an object containing a missing field are different cases.
summary: Find each edge of a range, then apply the same idea to rows and columns.

flow.title: Include the endpoint
flow.html:
A boundary is where a rule begins or ends. Inclusive means the endpoint belongs to the accepted range. For the range 1 through 4, both 1 and 4 must be accepted. Testing an ordinary middle value alone cannot establish that the endpoints were included correctly.

assertTrue(Numbers.allowed(4));

flow.title: Test the nearest value outside
flow.html:
For integer ranges, moving one step past an endpoint gives a useful nearby invalid value. Here 4 is accepted and 5 is rejected. Keeping this pair together exposes an upper-bound comparison that accepts one value too many or rejects the endpoint itself.

assertTrue(Numbers.allowed(4));
assertFalse(Numbers.allowed(5));

flow.title: Read an exclusive upper limit
flow.html:
An exclusive endpoint is different: the endpoint itself is outside the range. In 0 <= index && index < length, the largest valid integer index is length minus one. This is the rule Java arrays use. Read the comparison before selecting the expected boundary result.

LengthValid indexesFirst invalid upper index
30, 1, 23

flow.title: Vary the length
flow.html:
A sequence’s length is itself an input feature. An empty array has no first element. A one-element array has only index zero. A longer array can expose behaviour that requires continuation. These shapes provide different test situations even before you vary the elements stored inside them.

new int[0]
new int[]{7}
new int[]{7, 9}

flow.title: Give rows their own range
flow.html:
A grid adds a second coordinate, but the index rule stays the same. Begin with rows only. A grid with 2 rows permits row 0 and row 1. Hold the column at a valid value while testing the row edge, so a bad column cannot explain the result.

Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
assertFalse(grid.contains(2, 0));

flow.title: Give columns their own range
flow.html:
Now keep the row valid and examine columns. The same 2 by 4 grid permits columns 0 through 3. Column 4 is the first invalid upper value. Row and column counts are separate facts: changing one must not silently change the other coordinate’s boundary.

Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
assertFalse(grid.contains(1, 4));

flow.title: Choose an unequal shape
flow.html:
A square grid can hide confusion between its dimensions because its row and column counts are equal. A non-square grid makes that confusion visible. In a 2 by 4 grid, column 3 is valid although row 3 would not be. Choose an observation that depends on the difference.

Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
assertTrue(grid.contains(1, 3));

flow.title: Write a boundary test with one purpose
flow.html:
Put the established pieces into one test: construct the non-square shape, make the boundary call, and assert the promised result. A descriptive method name identifies the edge under test. You already know the syntax; the new work is selecting a case that makes the dimension rule observable.

@Test void lastColumn_isValid() {
    Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
    assertTrue(grid.contains(1, 3));
}

title: Distinguish null, empty and malformed objects
goals: Distinguish null references, empty values and null fields.
Match concrete arguments to String, array and object parameters.
Avoid inventing behaviour for unspecified inputs.
setup: null means that a reference does not refer to an object. "" is an existing String with length zero. new int[0] is an existing array with no elements. An object whose field is null is still an object. These distinctions matter because the contract can assign different outcomes to each.
bridge: Some methods depend on the object’s history as well as their immediate arguments. Next, test operations and state together.
summary: Distinguish a missing reference from the different values a real object can contain.

flow.title: Separate null from an empty String
flow.html:
Null means there is no String object at that reference. The empty String is an existing object whose length is zero. A contract may give both cases the same result, but they remain different inputs. Here lengthOrZero explicitly accepts null; do not assume null must always cause rejection.

Names.lengthOrZero(null)
Names.lengthOrZero("")

flow.title: Treat spaces according to the contract
flow.html:
A blank-looking String can still contain characters. In this contract, spaces count; no trimming is promised. Three spaces therefore produce length three. A test should not quietly replace “empty” with “blank” or assume that a method removes whitespace just because that behaviour might be useful elsewhere.

assertEquals(3, Names.lengthOrZero("   "));

flow.title: Separate an object from its field
flow.html:
A Contact object stores a String field named name. The object can exist even when that field is null. The constructor shown accepts its argument as given; it adds no validation. Compare a missing Contact with a constructed Contact whose name is missing: they are different levels of absence.

Contact absent = null;
Contact unnamed = new Contact(null);

flow.title: Construct the state you intend
flow.html:
Use the constructor to make each reference case explicit. A missing object, a missing field and an empty field can challenge different contract rules. The signature alone does not decide their outcomes. For now, practise constructing the states accurately before deciding how a method should respond to them.

Contact emptyName = new Contact("");

flow.title: Separate array absence from array length
flow.html:
Arrays are references too. A null array supplies no array object. A zero-length array exists but contains no elements. An int array with one zero has one element, whose value is zero. Keep object existence, number of elements and element values separate when choosing cases.

null
new int[0]
new int[]{0}

flow.title: Inspect a reference element
flow.html:
A String array stores String references. Its elements can therefore be null even when the array itself exists. This is different from int arrays, whose individual elements are primitive ints. When a method processes String entries, a null element is another concrete case to consider under its contract.

String[] names = new String[]{null};

flow.title: Distinguish malformed contents from a wrong type
flow.html:
A String can have the correct Java type and still violate a content rule. Suppose a code must contain exactly two characters. "A" fits the parameter type but fails that length rule. The integer 12 does not fit the String parameter at all. These faults occur at different stages.

/** True exactly for non-null Strings of length 2. */
static boolean validCode(String code)

flow.title: Stop where the promise stops
flow.html:
A precondition can restrict a method’s supported inputs without defining a rejection policy. If sum requires a non-null, nonempty array, that statement alone does not promise a particular result or exception for null. You can investigate such a call, but cannot label one guessed outcome as the required contract behaviour.

/** Requires a non-null, nonempty array; returns its sum. */
static int sum(int[] values)

flow.title: Combine the reference cases
flow.html:
Now make a small case table for a method that explicitly handles reference details. The rule below counts only entries that exist and contain at least one character. Work through the array and count qualifying entries. This combines the absence and length distinctions you have just practised.

// Contract: ignore null and empty entries; count all others.
Names.countPresent(new String[]{null, "", "Ada"})

title: Test an abstract data type through its operations
goals: Explain an ADT independently of its storage representation.
Distinguish an ADT from a Java abstract class or interface.
Test returned values and observable state across a sequence.
setup: An abstract data type (ADT) describes values and operations by their behaviour. A queue stores a sequence and removes the oldest inserted item: first in, first out (FIFO). The concept does not require an array, linked nodes or a particular Java class. An implementation chooses storage while preserving that public behaviour.
bridge: You can observe objects now. Next, decide whether a test needs equal values, the same object, or a particular ordering.
summary: Follow a queue’s behaviour before connecting it to Java’s abstraction tools.

flow.title: Describe behaviour without storage
flow.html:
An abstract data type, or ADT, describes values and operations by what they do. A queue keeps items in arrival order. Its rules do not choose arrays or linked nodes as storage. Start with this behaviour, because tests can observe it without inspecting the representation.

Queue operationPromise
Add an itemPlace it after existing items
Remove an itemReturn and remove the oldest item

flow.title: Observe first in, first out
flow.html:
The oldest item is the one added earliest among the items still present. This queue rule is called first in, first out, or FIFO. If A arrives before B, the first removal must return A. The order is part of the promise, not an optional detail.

OperationContents afterward
Add A[A]
Add B[A, B]
Remove, returning A[B]

flow.title: Observe state as well as a return
flow.html:
A removal promises two things: a returned item and a changed queue. A broken method could return A but leave it stored. Checking the size after removal gives another observation. The queue’s starting state therefore matters just as much as the written arguments to an operation.

Starting contentsActionRequired returnRequired size
[A, B]RemoveA1

flow.title: Trace a sequence of operations
flow.html:
Each operation begins with the state left by the preceding operation. Keep the oldest item on the left of your written queue. Trace an add, then a removal, then another add. This makes the expected state explicit instead of assuming that each call starts with an empty queue.

OperationContents afterward
Add A[A]
Remove A[]
Add B[B]

flow.title: Distinguish a Java interface
flow.html:
A Java interface declares operations that an implementing class must provide. It is a language tool that can describe an ADT’s operations. The small interface below names an add and a remove operation, but supplies neither stored items nor method bodies. An interface is not the same concept as an ADT.

interface NameQueue {
    void add(String item);
    String remove();
}

flow.title: Distinguish an abstract class
flow.html:
A Java abstract class is a class marked abstract. It cannot be directly instantiated; a concrete subclass—a class extending it—can supply a usable implementation. It can hold instance state and implemented methods. The word abstract here is Java syntax, not a requirement imposed by every ADT.

abstract class QueueBase {
    int size;
}

flow.title: State the collection’s element type
flow.html:
Java’s ArrayDeque is a concrete collection we can use as a queue. In ArrayDeque<String>, the angle brackets specify the element type: String. This is a generic type. The declaration below names a reference; it does not create the collection yet. A String collection does not accept an int element.

ArrayDeque<String> queue;

flow.title: Choose a concrete implementation
flow.html:
Deque is Java’s interface for a collection usable at either end. ArrayDeque supplies a concrete implementation. The variable below is described through the interface, while new constructs the concrete object. Both declarations use String elements. Imports make these library names available just as imports made JUnit names available earlier.

import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.ArrayDeque;

Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<String>();

flow.title: Use the queue operations
flow.html:
We use this deque as a FIFO queue by pairing two operations. addLast appends a String and returns void. removeFirst removes and returns the oldest String. These are the concrete Java names for the operations you already traced. The queue below is newly constructed and initially empty.

queue.addLast("A");
queue.addLast("B");
String actual = queue.removeFirst();

flow.title: Read the collection’s size
flow.html:
The method size() returns an int count, and isEmpty() returns whether that count is zero. These are observations, so they do not add or remove items. After removing the only item, either observation can check the promised empty state; choose the assertion that matches its returned type.

assertEquals(0, queue.size());
assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());

flow.title: Test reuse after becoming empty
flow.html:
A sequence can check that a structure still works after a transition. Drain the queue, then use it again. This reuses the construction, FIFO, return-value and empty-state skills already taught. A fresh local queue keeps the sequence independent of every other test.

queue.addLast("A");
assertEquals("A", queue.removeFirst());
assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());

practice.title: Describe behaviour without storage
practice.prompt: A queue ADT promises that removing an item returns the oldest item. Does that promise require its implementation to store the items in an array?
practice.hint: Separate what the operation does from how it stores data.
practice.solution: The queue’s behaviour can be implemented with different storage choices.

options.text: No; the promise specifies behaviour, not storage.
options.feedback: A different representation can preserve the same queue rules.

options.text: Yes; ADT means array data type.
options.feedback: ADT means abstract data type, and does not require an array.

practice.title: Observe first in, first out
practice.prompt: A fresh FIFO queue receives A, then B. What must the first removal return?
practice.hint: Choose the oldest remaining item.
practice.solution: The first removal must return A.

options.feedback: A arrived before B and has not yet been removed.
Removing the newest item first would be stack behaviour.
FIFO specifies the removal order.

practice.title: Observe state as well as a return

title: Choose equality, identity and ordering checks
goals: Distinguish object identity from value equality.
Use appropriate expectations for arrays and BigInteger results.
Test compareTo by sign unless exact values are promised.
setup: Objects create several different questions. Are these references pointing to one object? Do two objects represent equal values? Does one object sort before another? The assertion must ask the same question as the contract. A test can compile and still use the wrong notion of sameness.
bridge: So far the contract selected the cases. Next, read an implementation to find additional paths that deserve tests.
summary: Choose value equality, object identity or ordering as three different observations.

flow.title: Check a String’s value
flow.html:
Two objects can represent the same text. For Strings, assertEquals checks their character contents. The expected String below comes from the contract, while actual holds the returned value. This is a value question; it does not require the result to be a particular String object.

assertEquals("Ada", actual);

flow.title: Check the exact object
flow.html:
Identity asks whether two references point to the same object. The assignment below copies a reference, so saved and original identify one object. assertSame tests that property. It is appropriate when a method promises to return the exact object it received, rather than merely an equal value.

String original = new String("Ada");
String saved = original;
assertSame(original, saved);

flow.title: Check array contents separately
flow.html:
Two separately constructed arrays can contain the same elements. Ordinary array equals does not compare those elements. Use assertArrayEquals for contents, and assertNotSame only when a distinct array is also promised. One check cannot replace the other because content and identity are separate properties.

assertArrayEquals(new int[]{2, 4}, actual);
assertNotSame(source, actual);

flow.title: Keep a BigInteger expectation in its type
flow.html:
The digits printed by a value do not fully describe its type. A BigInteger with value seven is not equal to an Integer with value seven. Construct the expected BigInteger before comparing. An int expected value can compile through an object overload and still be the wrong equality check.

assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(7), actual);

flow.title: Check a custom object through its contract
flow.html:
A custom class may not define value equality. Java’s default Object equality checks identity. If an API does not supply a value-equality rule, two objects with matching fields need not satisfy assertEquals. Use documented observers to check the promised values instead of assuming every field will be compared automatically.

assertEquals(4, counter.get());

flow.title: Read the sign of compareTo
flow.html:
compareTo expresses ordering. Its general contract uses a negative result for before, zero for equal ordering, and a positive result for after. It does not generally promise exactly -1 or 1. For Strings, the call below asks whether "A" sorts before "D".

assertTrue("A".compareTo("D") < 0);

flow.title: Change a field that ordering must ignore
flow.html:
A useful equal-order case can contain different objects. Suppose Ticket compares only priority and must ignore label. Give two Tickets equal priority but different labels. A zero result then tests the “priority only” rule; two completely identical Tickets would not expose an accidental label tie-breaker.

Ticket a = new Ticket(5, "A");
Ticket b = new Ticket(5, "Z");
assertEquals(0, a.compareTo(b));

flow.title: Test the opposite ordering direction
flow.html:
This Ticket contract orders priorities in ascending order. The same sign rule works in the other direction. Give the receiver a larger priority and the argument a smaller one. Expect a positive result. You now have three separate ordering cases: lower, equal and higher. Write the expected relation first, then choose a comparison that expresses it.

assertTrue(high.compareTo(low) > 0);

title: Trace branches and short-circuit conditions
goals: Distinguish statement, branch and condition coverage.
Trace which operands are actually evaluated with && and ||.
State the measured coverage denominator without treating coverage as proof.
setup:
White-box testing uses the implementation’s structure to select cases: decisions, paths and loops. The contract still determines what ought to happen. Coverage records which measured parts were exercised. It does not tell you whether the assertions were strong or whether the contract was implemented correctly.

For this lesson, a decision is the complete boolean test controlling an if or loop; an outcome is true or false. A condition is one boolean part of that decision, such as member or points >= 100. An operand is a part supplied to an operator: in A && B, A and B are operands. We will count explicitly named outcomes, so “covered” always has a stated meaning.
bridge: Branches choose paths. Loops repeat paths, introducing empty cases, off-by-one errors and failures to make progress.
summary: Measure statements, decisions and evaluated conditions one at a time.

flow.title: Choose a case from the code
flow.html:
White-box testing uses the implementation’s structure to choose cases. In this method, the if condition suggests trying a positive count and a nonpositive count. The contract still decides the expected results. Reading a branch helps choose an input; it does not make the current implementation its own oracle.

static int flag(int count) {
    int result = 0;             // S1
    if (count > 0) {
        result = 1;            // S2
    }
    return result;             // S3
}

flow.title: Count executed statements
flow.html:
Statement coverage asks which measured executable statements ran. For this exercise, count only the three marked assignment/return statements S1, S2 and S3. A positive count executes all three. A nonpositive count skips S2. Name the measured statements so the denominator of your fraction is explicit.

static int flag(int count) {
    int result = 0;             // S1
    if (count > 0) {
        result = 1;            // S2
    }
    return result;             // S3
}

flow.title: Count decision outcomes
flow.html:
Branch coverage here counts the true and false outcomes of the single if decision. That gives two outcomes to cover. A test with count 1 reaches the true outcome but misses the false one, even though all three marked statements ran. Statement coverage and branch coverage ask different questions.

InputDecision outcome
1true
0false

flow.title: Write the missing branch case
flow.html:
To cover the missing outcome, choose a value that makes the condition false. Zero is especially useful when the contract changes at zero. Then add an assertion for the required result. Reaching a route without observing its result would still leave the test unable to detect a wrong returned value.

assertEquals(0, Numbers.flag(0));

flow.title: Read a negated emptiness check
flow.html:
The shipping method will also need a nonempty name. String.isEmpty() returns true when the String has zero characters. The prefix ! reverses a Boolean result. Therefore !name.isEmpty() says the name has at least one character. Assume the String is non-null for this small example.

String name = "Ada";
boolean hasName = !name.isEmpty();

flow.title: Combine the three shipping requirements
flow.html:
We now apply the same decision idea to a shipping query. Its one if combines three conditions with &&: the name exists, the name is nonempty, and count is positive. Label them A, B and C. The whole decision succeeds only when all three conditions evaluate true.

static boolean canShip(String name, int count) {
    if (name != null && !name.isEmpty() && count > 0) {
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

flow.title: Record a skipped condition honestly
flow.html:
With &&, Java stops evaluating as soon as a condition is false. For a null name, A is false, so B and C are skipped. A skipped condition is neither an observed true nor an observed false. This distinction is essential when counting which condition outcomes a suite actually exercised.

ArgumentsA: name != nullB: !name.isEmpty()C: count > 0
null, 1falseskippedskipped

flow.title: Count condition outcomes
flow.html:
Condition coverage counts true and false evaluations of each individual condition. Here three conditions have two possible outcomes each, giving six tracked outcomes. The pair null/1 and Ada/1 covers both whole-decision outcomes, but B and C are only observed true. Their false outcomes still need their own cases.

CaseABC
null, 1falseskippedskipped
"Ada", 1truetruetrue

flow.title: Complete the evaluated-condition table
flow.html:
Choose inputs that reach each later condition before making it false. An empty non-null name reaches B; a nonempty name with count zero reaches C. Alongside null and a fully valid call, these cases observe every tracked outcome. The decision denominator remains two, while the condition denominator remains six.

ArgumentsDecision
null, 1false
"", 1false
"Ada", 0false
"Ada", 1true

flow.title: Use coverage as evidence of execution
flow.html:
Coverage tells you what ran under a stated measure. It does not establish that the contract is right, that every assertion is useful, or that all input values are correct. A suite can reach every branch and then check only assertTrue(true). Keep meaningful expected results alongside the coverage information.

canShip("Ada", 1);
assertTrue(true);

title: Test loops and explain why they stop
goals: Trace loop initialization, condition, body and update.
Select zero-, one- and multiple-iteration cases with useful element positions.
Explain an off-by-one, early-return or nontermination defect using a concrete trace.
setup: A loop adds two questions: how many times does the body run, and does each repetition make progress? Start by locating initialization, condition, body and update. For finite arrays, empty, one-element and longer inputs expose different control-flow situations. Position matters as well as length.
bridge: You now have many possible tests. Next, organize them so each adds useful evidence and failures point to a specific rule.
summary: Use progressively longer searches to expose loop and return mistakes.

flow.title: Start with zero iterations
flow.html:
Searches.firstIndex looks for a target in an array and returns its first index, or -1 if absent. An empty array contains no match and gives a zero-iteration case for the usual indexed loop. The initial index is zero, and zero is not less than a length of zero.

Searches.firstIndex(new int[0], 7)

flow.title: Check one successful iteration
flow.html:
A one-element array adds one reachable body execution. If that element matches, the method should return index zero. This checks an immediate success but says nothing about moving to a later index. Keep the array index separate from the element’s value when choosing the expected result.

assertEquals(0, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{7}, 7));

flow.title: Check one unsuccessful iteration
flow.html:
Now change only the element so the single comparison fails. The search must finish the loop and return -1 afterward. This case checks a non-match without requiring a second iteration. A complete test distinguishes successful and unsuccessful single-element searches, even though the array lengths are the same.

assertEquals(-1, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{4}, 7));

flow.title: Require the search to continue
flow.html:
A match after an initial non-match requires another iteration. The faulty method below returns -1 inside the loop, so it stops after inspecting only the first element. A first-position match would hide that defect. Choose a later match to make the missing continuation observable.

static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] == target) { return i; }
        return -1;
    }
    return -1;
}

flow.title: Check the first of several matches
flow.html:
The word first is a separate requirement. With duplicate targets, several indexes match but only the earliest is allowed. A search that keeps overwriting a saved index could accidentally return the last match. Use repeated values to distinguish that behaviour from the promised first-match result.

assertEquals(0, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{7, 4, 7}, 7));

flow.title: Trace the first index outside the array
flow.html:
The loop must stop before index equals length. Changing < to <= lets an unsuccessful search attempt one more access. For a one-element array, index zero is valid and index one is not. Tracing that next iteration explains the resulting ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException precisely.

for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) { return i; }
}

flow.title: Find the loop’s progress measure
flow.html:
A loop must change the state that will eventually end it. In the indexed search, i should move toward values.length. The while loop below never changes i. If the first element does not match, the same comparison repeats forever under this unchanged state; a later match is never reached.

int i = 0;
while (i < values.length) {
    if (values[i] == target) { return i; }
}

flow.title: Interpret a timeout cautiously
flow.html:
A test can have a time budget. Exceeding it shows that the run did not finish within that budget; it does not alone explain why. The preceding unchanged-index trace supports a nontermination diagnosis. A different run might be slow or waiting. Use a concrete control-flow explanation alongside the timing observation.

ObservationWhat it establishes
Time budget exceededNo completion within that limit
Index never changes on a repeating pathA specific reason this loop cannot progress

flow.title: Write a last-position witness
flow.html:
A last-position match requires the search to continue through earlier non-matches and still inspect the final valid index. Write one test that makes that requirement concrete. This combines the loop, position and independent-expectation skills already practised, using a small input whose result is easy to verify by hand.

Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{4, 9, 7}, 7)

Isolate parameter failures before combining invalid inputs.

setup: A test suite is a collection of tests. Its value comes from the distinct behaviours it challenges. Several tests can share a result while exposing different faults. Conversely, many tests can repeat the same ordinary case. Build a small coverage table before writing methods.

flow.title: Give each test a purpose
flow.html:
A suite is a collection of tests. Organize it by what each case challenges, rather than by how many calls it contains. The shipping contract needs a valid case, missing and empty names, and a nonpositive count. Each row should pair concrete arguments with a required result and a reason.

flow.html:
A call with two invalid inputs can be rejected even if one required check is missing. With a null name and count zero, rejecting the name already produces false. That observation cannot establish that the count was checked. Keep the other inputs valid when targeting one restriction.

flow.html:

assertFalse(Shipping.canShip("Ada", 0));

flow.html:

For a case directly specified by the contract, no invented assumption is needed. The comment should explain the selection rather than repeat every Java statement.

// Design: black-box case from the documented name rule.

static int flags(boolean a, boolean b) {
    int result = 0;
    if (a) { result += 1; }
    if (b) { result += 2; }
    return result;
}

flow.title: Separate paths from branch outcomes
flow.html:
The all-false and all-true cases make each if take both outcomes across the suite. Under our source-level measure, that covers four of four branch outcomes. if (x < 0) { /* second branch */ }

title: Trace throw, catch and finally
goals: Explain throw, throws, try, catch and finally in a concrete trace.
Distinguish normal return from exceptional completion.
Recognize checked exceptions and unreachable catch ordering.
setup: Follow the familiar Counter validation helper through normal completion, throw, try, catch, and finally. Introduce each control-flow statement before combining them in a trace.
bridge: Now express “this exact call must throw this kind of exception” as a JUnit assertion.
summary: Follow one validation failure through Java’s exception-control statements.

flow.title: Separate normal and exceptional completion
flow.html:
Our Counter helper checks a value without changing an object. For a nonnegative value, the void call completes normally. For a negative value, it throws IllegalArgumentException instead. Throwing interrupts the normal sequence; the statement after the call does not simply continue as if the check had succeeded.

Counter.requireNonnegative(-1);

flow.title: Throw an exception object
flow.html:
The throw statement throws a particular exception object. The familiar new syntax constructs that object; its String argument supplies a message describing the problem. The line below belongs to the negative-value path of our helper. It creates and throws the failure at that point, rather than returning a numeric result.

throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");

flow.title: Use small output markers to trace control
flow.html:
We will use printed letters to show which statements execute. System.out.print writes the supplied text without automatically adding a new line. It returns void. These letters are observation markers, not part of the validation policy. Read them in execution order to trace normal and exceptional paths.

System.out.print("A");
System.out.print("B");

flow.title: Locate the try block
flow.html:
A try/catch statement pairs code to attempt with a possible handler. The try block contains the operation being attempted. The supplied catch clause handles a matching failure if one occurs. Both blocks use braces. Start by locating where the ordinary operation is placed; no extra function is created by try.

try {
    Counter.requireNonnegative(0);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("caught");
}

flow.title: Read the catch header
flow.html:
The catch header names an exception type and a variable. Here IllegalArgumentException is the type handled, and ex refers to the thrown object when that handler runs. The catch body executes for a matching exception; it does not execute just because the try block has finished successfully.

catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("C");
}

flow.title: Trace the normal path
flow.html:
When the helper receives zero, it completes normally. Execution therefore continues with the next statement in try. No exception selects the catch body, so its marker is skipped. Trace one statement at a time, separating code that is present in the source from code reached by this call.

try {
    System.out.print("A");
    Counter.requireNonnegative(0);
    System.out.print("B");
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("C");
}

flow.title: Trace the exceptional path
flow.html:
Changing the supplied value to -1 changes the route. A prints, then the validation throws. B is skipped because normal execution of that try path has been interrupted. The matching catch prints C. If that handler completes normally, execution can continue after the whole try/catch statement.

try {
    System.out.print("A");
    Counter.requireNonnegative(-1);
    System.out.print("B");
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("C");
}

flow.title: Run finally on the way out
flow.html:
A finally block runs as execution leaves the try/catch on ordinary or exceptional paths. It is commonly used for exit work. Here it only prints D so you can observe its position. This rule concerns normal Java control transfer; abruptly terminating the entire JVM is a different situation.

try {
    System.out.print("A");
    Counter.requireNonnegative(0);
    System.out.print("B");
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("C");
} finally {
    System.out.print("D");
}

flow.title: Propagate an unhandled exception
flow.html:
A catch must match the thrown type. A NullPointerException handler does not handle this IllegalArgumentException. The failure therefore propagates to the caller after any finally block runs. A statement after this try statement is skipped on that exceptional path; the code does not resume there merely because finally executed.

try {
    Counter.requireNonnegative(-1);
} catch (NullPointerException ex) {
    System.out.print("C");
} finally {
    System.out.print("D");
}
System.out.print("E");

flow.title: Rethrow the caught object
flow.html:
A handler can throw again instead of finishing normally. throw ex; rethrows the same exception object named by the catch variable. After the handler’s work, the failure continues outward; it is not automatically erased by entering catch. The finally block still runs on the way out.

try {
    Counter.requireNonnegative(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("C");
    throw ex;
} finally {
    System.out.print("D");
}

flow.title: Distinguish throws from throw
flow.html:
A method header can declare possible propagation using throws. This declaration does not throw anything by itself. The executed body determines whether an exception occurs. Our helper can declare IllegalArgumentException and still complete normally for zero. Keep the plural header keyword separate from the singular executable throw statement.

static void requireNonnegative(int value)
        throws IllegalArgumentException

flow.title: Recognize the checked-exception rule
flow.html:
Java requires calling code to catch or declare a checked exception, such as IOException when reading stored data. IllegalArgumentException and NullPointerException are unchecked, so that compiler requirement does not apply to them. Here, java.io.IOException is the full type name, so it needs no import. The wrapper declares that checked exception and lets it propagate.

static String readName() throws java.io.IOException {
    return Names.readSaved();
}

flow.title: Put a specific handler before a broad one
flow.html:
IllegalArgumentException is a subclass of Exception: an Exception handler also matches it. If the broad handler comes first, the later specific handler can never be selected, so Java rejects that ordering. Put the specific handler first when both are needed. This is a compilation issue, before any trace can run.

try {
    Counter.requireNonnegative(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("specific");
} catch (Exception ex) {
    System.out.print("general");
}

title: Write precise exception tests
goals: Write assertThrows with a class literal and an executable lambda.
Check a documented exception message separately from JUnit’s failure message.
Avoid a false positive caused by a different operation throwing.
setup: Use Counter.set to build a JUnit exception check from a delayed action and an exception type. Then inspect the documented message and unchanged state.
bridge: Next, read and repair manual try/catch tests, then apply the same contract discipline to defensive code and defect reports.
summary: Build an exception assertion from its smallest syntax pieces, then check its scope and observations.

flow.title: Describe an operation to run later
flow.html:
For an exception test, JUnit must invoke the operation while observing it. A lambda supplies an operation to run later. The empty parentheses mean it takes no input of its own; the arrow introduces its action. This fragment describes the call without performing it immediately. counter already refers to a valid Counter object here.

() -> counter.set(-1)

flow.title: Name an exception type with .class
flow.html:
JUnit also needs the expected exception type. The expression IllegalArgumentException.class is a class literal identifying that type. It is not a quoted message and does not construct an exception. You are telling the assertion what kind of failure it should look for when it invokes the supplied operation.

IllegalArgumentException.class

flow.title: Combine the type and delayed operation
flow.html:
assertThrows takes the expected type, then the delayed operation. It invokes the lambda and checks the exception that escapes it. The call below checks one negative set on an already constructed Counter. Both ingredients were introduced separately: a class literal identifies the type, and the lambda supplies the operation.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> counter.set(-1));

flow.title: Distinguish the assertion’s outcomes
flow.html:
An exception assertion can fail in two basic ways: the operation returns normally, or it throws the wrong kind of exception. It succeeds when the required exception kind occurs. Thus an expected exception is evidence of success for this test, not automatically a failed test run.

Observed operation outcomeassertThrows expecting IllegalArgumentException
Normal completionFails
NullPointerExceptionFails
IllegalArgumentExceptionPasses

flow.title: Read a lambda with a block body
flow.html:
A lambda can also use braces for a block of statements. Each statement inside the block ends with its usual semicolon. The closing brace ends the lambda body. This is the same delayed-operation idea; braces only allow a block instead of the single call expression used earlier.

() -> {
    counter.set(-1);
}

flow.title: Keep the observed operation narrow
flow.html:
If several operations sit inside the lambda, an earlier one may throw the expected type before the intended target is reached. That can produce a misleading pass. Establish valid setup outside the assertion and keep the target call inside. Here the helper throws before set, so set is not actually tested.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
    Counter.requireNonnegative(-5);
    counter.set(-1);
});

flow.title: Keep the returned exception object
flow.html:
When assertThrows succeeds, it returns the exception object that was thrown. You can store that result in a variable, just as you store a method’s returned int or String. The variable below has the exception type. It is not a pass/fail Boolean, and storing it does not throw it again.

IllegalArgumentException ex = assertThrows(
    IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> counter.set(-1));

flow.title: Check a promised exception message
flow.html:
The exception method getMessage() returns its message as a String. Check it only when the contract promises particular text or another message property. Our negative set contract promises the exact sentence below, so an ordinary String equality assertion can check that separate observation after assertThrows has returned ex.

assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());

flow.title: Separate JUnit’s diagnostic message
flow.html:
The optional third argument of assertThrows is JUnit’s explanation if its assertion fails. It is not the expected exception message. The phrase below tells you why the test expected rejection. To check the thrown object’s own message, use the separate getMessage assertion you just practised.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> counter.set(-1), "Negative values must be rejected");

flow.title: Recognize accepted subtypes
flow.html:
A subclass is also a member of its superclass type. NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException. Therefore assertThrows expecting IllegalArgumentException also accepts NumberFormatException. This is the same kind of type relationship that allowed a broad catch handler to match a more specific exception in the previous lesson.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
    throw new NumberFormatException("bad number");
});

flow.title: Ask for an exact type only when promised
flow.html:
assertThrowsExactly requires the thrown exception’s class to be exactly the requested class. It does not accept a subclass. Use that stricter requirement only when the contract actually promises it. Requiring exact classes without a reason can reject behaviour that a broader documented exception contract allows.

assertThrowsExactly(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> counter.set(-1));

flow.title: Check a valid input too
flow.html:
A method that rejects every input could pass a suite containing only rejection tests. assertDoesNotThrow checks that a delayed operation completes normally. For a mutating method, also inspect the promised state afterward. This accepted zero case complements the negative cases instead of merely adding another rejection.

assertDoesNotThrow(() -> counter.set(0));
assertEquals(0, counter.get());

flow.title: Combine rejection with unchanged state
flow.html:
A rejection contract may promise that existing state survives the failure. Arrange a valid value first, perform one rejected set, then inspect the observer. You have already learned every part: local fixture, delayed operation, expected exception and value assertion. This complete test combines them for one coherent behaviour.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);
assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> counter.set(-1));
assertEquals(4, counter.get());
